The first they call rational proof.
The second they call transmitted proof, or proof from an authoritative text.
Their rational proof has three parts.
First, they argue that the imam must be protected from error, like the Prophet, so that he can safely carry the responsibility for preserving religious belief and law after the Prophet.
The Shiʿa then say that when the Prophet died, no one except ʿAlī possessed this protection from error. Therefore, ʿAlī had to be the imam.
Second, they argue that an imam must be someone who has never committed a sin. Since ʿAlī had never worshipped idols before Islam, they conclude that he must have been the imam.

Third, they argue that the imam must be more knowledgeable than anyone else in his own time. They believe that ʿAlī was exactly that. Therefore, in their view, he had to be the imam rather than anyone else.
Sunnis reject all three of these claims as rational proofs.
They argue that no one has proved that an imam must be protected from error, that he must never previously have committed a sin, or that he must be the most learned person of his time.

For Sunnis, it is enough that the person has the necessary qualifications to carry out the responsibilities of the caliphate. He is then chosen by the ahl al-ḥall wa-l-ʿaqd—those recognized as having the authority to choose a ruler.
The Shiʿa’s other proof for ʿAlī’s imamate comes from transmitted texts.
One is the well-known Hadith of Ghadīr, also called the Hadith of Mawlā.
According to the report, the Prophet was returning from Mecca to Medina after his final pilgrimage when he stopped at a place on the road called Ghadīr Khumm. A group of Companions was with him.
He stood before them and delivered a speech. Among other things, he asked:
“Do I not have a greater claim over you than you have over yourselves?”
The Prophet then took ʿAlī by the hand and said:
“God, whoever has me as his mawlā, ʿAlī is his mawlā. God, befriend whoever befriends him, oppose whoever opposes him, support whoever supports him, and abandon whoever abandons him.”
The Companions then came forward to congratulate ʿAlī, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
“Congratulations, ʿAlī. You have become my mawlā and the mawlā of every believing man and woman.”
Sunnis do not deny this hadith.
But they interpret it differently from the Shiʿa.
The disagreement centers on the word mawlā, which is the key word in the Shiʿi argument.
The Shiʿa understand it as referring to wilāya—authority, rule, or the imamate.
Sunnis understand it as walāʾ in the sense of love, loyalty, and friendship.
Under the Sunni interpretation, the hadith no longer serves as proof that the Prophet appointed ʿAlī as imam and ruler of the Muslims after him.

Al-Shahrastānī gives an initial definition of the religious and philosophical ideas that entered some Shiʿi beliefs about ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and took those groups beyond the basic position we described above.
Their beliefs moved into ghulūw—extremism—especially in the way they understood the person of ʿAlī and the imams descended from him.
“The extremists are those who went so far in what they claimed for their imams that they took them beyond the limits of created humanity and gave them divine qualities.
“Sometimes they compared one of the imams to God, and sometimes they compared God to created beings. In this way they moved between extremes of exaggeration and distortion.

“Their comparisons came from the doctrines of divine indwelling, from the doctrines of the transmigration of souls—the passing of a soul from one being into another—and from doctrines found among Jews and Christians.

“The Jews compared the Creator to created beings, while the Christians compared a created being to the Creator. These forms of comparison then entered the minds of the extremist Shiʿa until they began to give some of the imams divine qualities.
“This kind of comparison originally appeared among the Shiʿa, and only later returned among the Sunnis.”
Al-Shahrastānī therefore does more than give an initial definition of the theories of the extremist Alid groups.
He also tries to explain how these theories arose by tracing them back to their intellectual sources.

Does this mean, then, that ideas such as divine indwelling, the transmigration of souls, and similar doctrines already had a place in Arab thought during this period of Arab and Islamic history—or even before it?

We raise this question deliberately, because the answer will be useful when we later discuss the rise of philosophical thought and the development of Arab-Islamic philosophy itself. We will see that the theories mentioned by al-Shahrastānī also appear in some forms of that philosophy and in some of its ideas.

If our answer here shows that these theories already had roots in Arab-Islamic thought before philosophical thinking emerged, and before philosophy took shape as a distinct field, we will later be able to draw an important conclusion. Arab-Islamic philosophy, once it developed its own distinct place within Arab-Islamic thought, was not simply the result of importing Greek philosophy from outside. To a much greater extent, it grew out of a long historical process taking place within Arab life itself, as events interacted with religious thought and as that thought also came into contact with the achievements of world thought up to that time.
Let us now return to the question itself.

What we briefly discussed earlier, when looking at religious life in pre-Islamic Arabia, may help us answer it. We saw that Arab society at the time was already in contact with many of the religious ideas found among other peoples.

The Qurʾān itself provides evidence of this. It speaks about different religions and about various ways of explaining the universe, nature, and the realities of human life, whether through physical causes or unseen supernatural forces. The context makes clear that these were ideas already known among the pre-Islamic Arabs.
The Qurʾān mentions the “Magians” and the “Sabeans,” for example, in verse 17 of Sūrat al-Ḥajj:
“Those who believe, those who are Jews, the Sabeans, the Christians, the Magians, and those who associate others with God...”

Once we speak of the Magians and the Sabeans, we also have to remember the theories mentioned by al-Shahrastānī, including doctrines of divine indwelling, the transmigration of souls, and others like them.

We should also add what is historically known about the Arabs before Islam. They had already been influenced, though in a vague and unsystematic way, by Indian ideas and philosophy, as well as by ideas circulating in the Sasanian schools of Persia and Mesopotamia. This influence came through geographical contact and through trade, for which the Arabian Peninsula was one of the main routes in the pre-Islamic period.

Al-Yaʿqūbī confirms this when he discusses the religions of the pre-Islamic Arabs. Among them he mentions “dualism,” meaning the old Persian religion based on two divine principles. This was the doctrine of Manichaeism, which spoke of divine forces of good and evil. Al-Yaʿqūbī says that Ḥujr ibn ʿAmr al-Kindī followed this belief in the pre-Islamic period.

In the Islamic period, we have a great deal of historical evidence showing that the theories mentioned above already had living and developing roots in Arab-Islamic thought at the early stage we are discussing here—that is, from the seventh century and the beginning of the eighth century CE.

One especially revealing example appears in Ibn Abī al-Ḥadīd’s commentary on Nahj al-Balāgha. He tried to explain why the more extreme doctrines of certain Shiʿi groups became more widespread in Iraq and Iran than elsewhere. His explanation is important because, whatever its weaknesses, he tried to connect the phenomenon with the real conditions in which it developed.

“One difference that seems clear to me between these people and the Arabs who lived at the time of the Messenger of God is that these people are from Iraq and are inhabitants of Kufa. The soil of Iraq has always produced people of unusual doctrines and founders of novel sects. The people of this region are people of insight, close examination, reflection, and inquiry into ideas and beliefs, and into the objections raised against different doctrines. In the days of the Persian kings there had already appeared among them people such as Mani, Bardaisan, Mazdak, and others.

“The soil of the Hijaz is not like this, and neither are the minds of its people. The people of the Hijaz are generally marked by roughness, bluntness, and a certain harshness of character. Even those who live in its cities, such as Mecca, Medina, and Taʾif, have temperaments close to those of the neighboring Bedouins. Before this, there had been no sage or philosopher among them, no one devoted to speculation and debate, no one who raised such doubts, and no founder of a new doctrine.

“This is why we find that the teachings of the extremists appeared and developed only after ʿAlī settled in Iraq and Kufa, and not during the years he lived in Medina, which made up most of his life.”
The value of this passage is that Ibn Abī al-Ḥadīd traces the rise of extremism within Shiʿi thought back to its historical setting and to the conditions of the society in which it appeared.

When he compares the Hijaz with Iraq and points to the differences between them, he is trying to show the effect of Bedouin conditions in the Hijaz and urban conditions in Iraq. Those urban conditions had deep roots in Iraq’s earlier history and in its relationship with Persian civilization before the Arab-Islamic conquest.

In modern terms, his argument is roughly this: people in Iraq were more prepared to accept complex forms of metaphysical thought, while people in the Hijaz were less prepared to accept ideas of that level of complexity. This, in all likelihood, is what Ibn Abī al-Ḥadīd meant.
We agree with the method behind this explanation, but not with the explanation itself.

It is true that some of the more extreme Shiʿi doctrines began in Kufa, but they soon spread to Medina, then to many parts of the Arabian Peninsula, especially Yemen. We have also already seen that Indian and Persian philosophical ideas had left traces in Arabia even before Islam.
The name “Kaysāniyya” refers to the first of the Shiʿi groups regarded as extremist.
The group was named after Kaysān, a mawlā—a non-Arab client—of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. After studying under ʿAlī, Kaysān became a follower of ʿAlī’s son Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya.
Kaysān’s own followers were also mainly mawālī. They recognized Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya as imam, holding that the imamate had passed to him from his nephew ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.
Within a short time, however, the ideas of this group moved far away from the original foundations of Shiʿism.

They began to attribute qualities to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya that went far beyond normal human limits. They claimed that he possessed hidden knowledge of everything that had happened and everything that would happen. They also said that religion consisted in obeying a man who possessed all knowledge and understood the secrets of interpretation and the hidden inner meanings of things.
They later declared that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya would never truly die and that, after his apparent death, he would return to the earthly world.
Two features of this movement deserve particular attention.
The first is that its beliefs, especially the ideas of immortality and return, arose mainly among the mawālī of Kufa.

The group was named after Kaysān, himself a mawlā, as we have seen. After him came the followers of Abū ʿAmra, who was killed during the revolt led by al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī against the Umayyads in revenge for the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī.
Abū ʿAmra’s followers were also mawālī of Kufa. At that time, they belonged to one of the lowest-ranking social groups in Umayyad society.
It was these followers of Abū ʿAmra who were the first to say that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya would return after Abū ʿAmra was killed.

What makes this especially interesting is that they adopted this belief after their imam, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, had already made peace with the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, exchanged letters with him, and eventually recognized him as caliph. Earlier, he had also recognized Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya.

The mawālī were angry that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya had made peace with the Umayyads, whom they themselves had fought under the banner of al-Mukhtār al-Thaqafī. Al-Mukhtār had treated them as socially equal to the Arabs, without distinction.
They therefore saw Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya’s compromise as an abandonment of their cause, as well as of his own cause and that of the Prophet’s family.
Yet despite all this, they did not abandon their belief in him. On the contrary, their belief became more extreme.
They decided that he had committed a sin by making peace with the Umayyads, and that God had punished him by hiding him in a dark cave in Mount Raḍwā.

Before disappearing, they said, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya passed the imamate to his son Abū Hāshim. Abū Hāshim therefore became, in their eyes, the “silent imam” after the disappearance of the “speaking imam,” Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya.
Abū Hāshim then appointed no successor of his own. God, they believed, would return the imamate to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya when he came back after the period of his punishment was over.
Abū Khalaf al-Qummī reports them as saying:

“They know no authoritative guide other than him, cannot distinguish truth from what merely resembles it, or certainty from confusion, until God raises up the knowing imam, Muḥammad, known as Abū al-Qāsim”—meaning Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya himself—“in spite of all who oppose him and in spite of hostile time itself. He will rule the whole earth and wrench it from every defender.”
What can we learn from the story of these mawālī and from this belief of theirs?
Taken together, the details of the story and the belief in the imam’s return allow us to draw an important conclusion.

When the Kaysāni mawālī of Kufa—followers of Kaysān and Abū ʿAmra—joined al-Mukhtār’s revolt, they joined a movement that rejected the idea that their social position was naturally lower than that of the Arabs. Al-Mukhtār openly treated them as the Arabs’ equals.
On the surface, these men were fighting for the right of ʿAlī’s descendants to hold the imamate.

But beneath this visible political cause lay another form of social awareness. Without clearly realizing it themselves, they were also fighting for their own cause as an oppressed and despised group, subjected to many forms of humiliation and exploitation under the Umayyad state and under Arab tribal privilege.
That system of privilege was also used by the wealthy merchants and property owners of Kufa, many of whom descended from the rich merchants and property owners of pre-Islamic Mecca.
These mawālī saw in the descendants of ʿAlī, in their supporters, and in the Alid opposition to Umayyad rule a possible way out of the oppression and contempt they suffered.

Al-Mukhtār strengthened this hope within their still unclear social awareness. That hope first appeared in a religious and supernatural form, when they followed Kaysān and later Abū ʿAmra in supporting the imamate of Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya.
First, they saw their military leadership collapse with the death of al-Mukhtār, followed by the death of Abū ʿAmra.
